Reference: Pakes and McGuire (1994)

Model Setting

The paper develops a simple algorithm for computing Markov-perfect Nash equilibria of dynamic games among heterogeneous firms, and illustrates it with a differentiated-product version of the Ericson and Pakes (1995) model of industry dynamics. The motivation is empirical: firms in the same industry differ widely in the level and the evolution of market shares, investment and productivity, and entry and exit make their responses to policy nonlinear, so that even aggregate effects depend on the whole distribution of firms. In the model, firms invest to raise the quality of their product relative to an outside alternative, the outcome of investment is random, successful firms move to states with higher profits, and firms that fall behind eventually exit and are replaced by entrants. The general theory guarantees that an equilibrium exists and that the process for the industry structure is ergodic, but it says nothing about what the limit distribution looks like or how it responds to parameters. That is the role of computation.

The algorithm iterates jointly on the value function and the investment policy at every point of a finite state space, solving at each point a single equation in a single unknown, and it builds the solution up from the monopoly problem by raising the maximal number of active firms one at a time. With one set of parameter values the equilibrium has three or four active firms in almost all periods, simultaneous entry and exit in 13.1 percent of periods, a modal firm lifetime of one period against a mean of 18.4, and realized values that are negative for over 90 percent of entrants. The paper then compares the free-entry equilibrium with a social planner, a perfect cartel, temporary and permanent single-product monopoly, a cap on market share and a tenfold increase in the sunk cost of entry. The planner raises welfare by only about 2 percent but chooses a market structure that resembles the cartel's. A market-share cap leaves market structure almost unchanged and lowers welfare by over 5 percent, whereas the higher entry cost transforms market structure and barely changes welfare. Finally, the paper shows that the computational burden grows quickly with the number of firms and proposes polynomial approximations whose dimension is independent of that number once symmetry of the value function is imposed.

The entrant comes in at a fixed position relative to the outside alternative, so the ability of entrants advances at the pace of the outside world. Otherwise entry would eventually cease.

Three results of Ericson and Pakes shape the algorithm and are taken as given. First, for each sss there is an exit threshold below which the firm leaves and an upper threshold ωˉ(s)\bar{\omega}(s)ωˉ(s) above which investment is zero, because a bounded value function leaves no return to further increments. States above ωˉ(s)\bar{\omega}(s)ωˉ(s) are coasting states from which ω\omegaω can only drift down, so observed efficiencies lie in a finite set Ω={1,…,K}\Omega=\{1,\dots,K\}Ω={1,…,K}. Second, entry per period is bounded by some m∗m^*m∗. Third, there is an industry size N∗N^*N∗ at and above which nobody enters. Hence no more than N∗+m∗N^*+m^*N∗+m∗ firms are ever active and the set of attainable structures is finite:

S={s=[s1,…,sK]:∑jsj≤N∗+m∗},Pr⁡{st+1=s′∣st}=Pr⁡{st+1=s′∣st}≡Q[s′∣st](12)S=\left\{s=[s_1,\dots,s_K]:\sum_js_j\leq N^*+m^*\right\},\qquad\Pr\{s_{t+1}=s'\mid s^t\}=\Pr\{s_{t+1}=s'\mid s_t\}\equiv Q[s'\mid s_t] \tag{12}S={s=[s1​,…,sK​]:j∑​sj​≤N∗+m∗},Pr{st+1​=s′∣st}=Pr{st+1​=s′∣st​}≡Q[s′∣st​](12)

where sts^tst is the history of structures up to ttt. A Markov-perfect Nash equilibrium with rational expectations is a kernel QQQ such that, when every incumbent and potential entrant perceives the distribution of future structures to be the one derived from QQQ and chooses investment, exit and entry to maximize its expected discounted net cash flow, the objective distribution generated by those choices together with the distributions of τ\tauτ and of ωe\omega_eωe​ is QQQ itself. Strategies depend only on the payoff-relevant state (ω,s)(\omega,s)(ω,s). There may be more than one such QQQ. The process is ergodic: from any initial structure it enters a recurrent class in finite time, and sample averages converge to expectations under the invariant measure, although the structure itself never settles down.

The algorithm computes the investment policy x(ω,s)x(\omega,s)x(ω,s), the exit policy and the value of entry. It is easiest to describe as a sequence of problems in which at most NNN firms may be active, starting from N=1N=1N=1 and raising NNN until the limit no longer binds. With one firm the structure is just e(ω)e(\omega)e(ω) and the Bellman equation is:

Because a state that makes a monopolist exit also makes a firm with rivals exit, ω‾m\underline{\omega}^mω​m is a lower bound for the state space at every NNN. A fixed point l∗l^*l∗, together with the exit rule “stay if and only if l2∗>Φl^*_2>\Phil2∗​>Φ”, is a Markov-perfect Nash equilibrium of the game with at most two firms, because every agent then uses as beliefs the actual distribution of its competitors' future states and optimizes given those beliefs. Unlike the monopoly operator, this operator is not a contraction.

For N=3N=3N=3 the iteration starts from the two-firm solution, l0[ω1,ω2,ω3]=l∗{ω1,max⁡[ω2,ω3]}l^0[\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3]=l^*\{\omega_1,\max[\omega_2,\omega_3]\}l0[ω1​,ω2​,ω3​]=l∗{ω1​,max[ω2​,ω3​]}, and proceeds in the same way, except that none, one or both competitors may exit and zero, one or two entrants may follow. The procedure restarts at N+1N+1N+1 from the NNN-firm solution until it reaches an NNN such that Ve(s,1)<xeV^e(s,1)<x_eVe(s,1)<xe​ for every sss with NNN active firms. The smallest such NNN bounds the number of firms ever active. In practice the authors often stopped at an NNN where entry still occurred at a few such points, provided these points were absent or rare in the recurrent class.

Symmetry, Convergence and Computational Burden

Computing time is roughly the product of the time per grid point, the number of grid points and the number of iterations. Without further structure the number of grid points is kNk^NkN. Because a firm's value and policy do not depend on the order of its competitors, the value function is symmetric (exchangeable) in its last N−1N-1N−1 arguments:

V(ω1,ω2,…,ωN)=V(ω1,ωπ(2),…,ωπ(N))(20)V(\omega_1,\omega_2,\dots,\omega_N)=V(\omega_1,\omega_{\pi(2)},\dots,\omega_{\pi(N)}) \tag{20}V(ω1​,ω2​,…,ωN​)=V(ω1​,ωπ(2)​,…,ωπ(N)​)(20)

for any permutation π\piπ of (2,…,N)(2,\dots,N)(2,…,N), so it only needs to be computed at points with ω2≥ω3≥⋯≥ωN\omega_2\geq\omega_3\geq\dots\geq\omega_Nω2​≥ω3​≥⋯≥ωN​. The number of ordered sequences of length NNN with entries in [1,…,k][1,\dots,k][1,…,k] is:

S(k,N)=(k+N−1N)=(k+N−1)!(k−1)!N!(21)S(k,N)=\binom{k+N-1}{N}=\frac{(k+N-1)!}{(k-1)!N!} \tag{21}S(k,N)=(Nk+N−1​)=(k−1)!N!(k+N−1)!​(21)

(the paper prints KKK on the right-hand side), which grows as a polynomial in NNN (of order k−1k-1k−1; the paper says order kkk) and not exponentially. The grid actually used has a free own state and N−1N-1N−1 ordered competitors, hence k S(k,N−1)k\,S(k,N-1)kS(k,N−1) points. At each grid point the value function must still be evaluated at every structure reachable next period: with nnn continuing incumbents and binary increments there are 2n+12^{n+1}2n+1 of them without entry and as many with entry. Equilibria were computed for N=2,…,6N=2,\dots,6N=2,…,6. A six-firm equilibrium took about five hours on a Sun Sparc 1 workstation, time rose by a factor of about five with each additional firm, and the base case required the value function at 639,000 points.

Convergence is not guaranteed, and two sources of cycling were found. First, entry makes the incumbent's continuation value jump when the value of entry crosses the threshold, so iterations can alternate between entry and no entry at some states. The remedy is a version with random entry costs drawn from a continuous distribution Pce(⋅)P^{ce}(\cdot)Pce(⋅): when the value of entry is κ\kappaκ, incumbents perceive an entrant with probability Pce(κ)P^{ce}(\kappa)Pce(κ), which makes their policies smooth in the last iteration's value of entry. Second, when one of two firms must exit but either could, iterations can alternate between both exiting and both staying. The remedy orders exit decisions, with lower ω\omegaω deciding first, at the cost of a larger state space because firms at the same state must be distinguished. Dampening, that is, forming policies from a weighted average of the last several value functions, also worked well. Uniqueness is not guaranteed either, but the examples converged to the same fixed point from different starting values. Two alternatives were tried. A nested algorithm that solves a contraction for a best response to fixed beliefs and then updates beliefs has an inner fixed point of the same dimension as the outer one and is far more costly. Adding policy iteration steps (iterating on values at fixed policies) or value iteration steps (iterating on policies at a fixed value function) did not speed up the pointwise algorithm.

Planner and Cartel

Welfare is the discounted sum of net cash flows of active firms (profits minus investment), plus scrap values received minus entry costs paid, plus consumer surplus. With extreme value tastes the per-period consumer surplus with nnn active firms is printed as:

∫[max⁡j(ωj−pj+ϵj)]dG(ϵ1,…,ϵn)=log⁡∑jexp⁡(ωj−pj)(22)\int\left[\max_j\left(\omega_j-p_j+\epsilon_j\right)\right]dG(\epsilon_1,\dots,\epsilon_n)=\log\sum_j\exp(\omega_j-p_j) \tag{22}∫[jmax​(ωj​−pj​+ϵj​)]dG(ϵ1​,…,ϵn​)=logj∑​exp(ωj​−pj​)(22)

which is written in terms of ωj\omega_jωj​ and without the outside good's term, in contrast to the share equation. The social planner and the perfect cartel (a monopolist allowed to market any number of products) are single decision makers who control prices, investment, entry and exit of all products under the same technology, so their problems are ordinary dynamic programs. Let B(ω1,…,ωn)B(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n)B(ω1​,…,ωn​) be the current benefit. The planner sets every price equal to marginal cost and takes BBB from the consumer surplus formula. The cartel chooses prices to maximize joint profits:

max⁡(p1,…,pn)∑jMσ(ωj,pj;ω1,…,ωn,p1,…,pn)[pj−mc](23)\max_{(p_1,\dots,p_n)}\sum_jM\sigma(\omega_j,p_j;\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n,p_1,\dots,p_n)[p_j-mc] \tag{23}(p1​,…,pn​)max​j∑​Mσ(ωj​,pj​;ω1​,…,ωn​,p1​,…,pn​)[pj​−mc](23)

Ordering states so that ωi≤ωi−1\omega_i\leq\omega_{i-1}ωi​≤ωi−1​, the value function of either decision maker is computed by iterating on:

Vi(ω1,…,ωn)=max⁡q∈{1,…,n}Vˉi(ω1,…,ωq)(24)V^i(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n)=\max_{q\in\{1,\dots,n\}}\bar{V}^i(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q) \tag{24}Vi(ω1​,…,ωn​)=q∈{1,…,n}max​Vˉi(ω1​,…,ωq​)(24)

with:

Vˉi(ω1,…,ωq)=  B(ω1,…,ωq)+(n−q)Φ+max⁡{sup⁡(x1,…,xq)−c∑jxj+β∑Vi−1(ω1′,…,ωq′)p(ω1′∣ω1,x1,ν)⋯p(ωq′∣ωq,xq,ν)p(ν);sup⁡(x1,…,xq)−c∑jxj−xe+β∑Vi−1(ω1′,…,ωq′,ωe)p(ω1′∣ω1,x1,ν)⋯p(ωq′∣ωq,xq,ν)p(ωe∣ν)p(ν)}(25)\begin{aligned} \bar{V}^i(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)=\;&B(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)+(n-q)\Phi\\ &+\max\Big\{\sup_{(x_1,\dots,x_q)}-c\sum_jx_j+\beta\sum V^{i-1}(\omega'_1,\dots,\omega'_q)p(\omega'_1\mid\omega_1,x_1,\nu)\cdots p(\omega'_q\mid\omega_q,x_q,\nu)p(\nu);\\ &\sup_{(x_1,\dots,x_q)}-c\sum_jx_j-x_e+\beta\sum V^{i-1}(\omega'_1,\dots,\omega'_q,\omega_e)p(\omega'_1\mid\omega_1,x_1,\nu)\cdots p(\omega'_q\mid\omega_q,x_q,\nu)p(\omega_e\mid\nu)p(\nu)\Big\} \end{aligned} \tag{25}Vˉi(ω1​,…,ωq​)=​B(ω1​,…,ωq​)+(n−q)Φ+max{(x1​,…,xq​)sup​−cj∑​xj​+β∑Vi−1(ω1′​,…,ωq′​)p(ω1′​∣ω1​,x1​,ν)⋯p(ωq′​∣ωq​,xq​,ν)p(ν);(x1​,…,xq​)sup​−cj∑​xj​−xe​+β∑Vi−1(ω1′​,…,ωq′​,ωe​)p(ω1′​∣ω1​,x1​,ν)⋯p(ωq′​∣ωq​,xq​,ν)p(ωe​∣ν)p(ν)}​(25)

The outer maximum keeps the q∗q^*q∗ best products and scraps the remaining n−q∗n-q^*n−q∗. The inner maximum decides whether a new product is introduced next period at the entry cost xex_exe​. The paper prints the left-hand side with last argument ωi\omega_iωi​ and omits the discount factor β\betaβ in front of the continuation values; both are corrected here. The other regimes are variants of the Markov-perfect game: in the temporary monopoly the initial firm is alone for TTT periods, after which the free-entry equilibrium starts from sT+1=e(ωT+1)s_{T+1}=e(\omega_{T+1})sT+1​=e(ωT+1​); under the market-share cap each firm maximizes profit subject to σj≤σ∗\sigma_j\leq\sigma^*σj​≤σ∗, so a firm that would exceed the cap raises its price; under the licensing fee the sunk cost of entry is raised from 0.2 to 2.

Parameter Values and the Base Case

The base case uses δ=0.7\delta=0.7δ=0.7, β=0.925\beta=0.925β=0.925, xe=0.2x_e=0.2xe​=0.2, Φ=0.1\Phi=0.1Φ=0.1, M=5M=5M=5, a=3a=3a=3 and mc=5mc=5mc=5; the value of ccc is not listed. Production costs are about 25 per period, so the sunk cost of entry is about 1/125 of them and entry is cheap. With the monopolist's exit state normalized to one, the highest state with positive monopoly investment is 21. Entrants arrive at ω=3\omega=3ω=3 with probability δ\deltaδ and at ω=4\omega=4ω=4 with probability 1−δ1-\delta1−δ. Statistics come from one simulation of 10,000 periods starting with a single firm at ω=4\omega=4ω=4.

  • Market structure: three firms are active in 63.0 percent of periods, four in 35.3, five in 1.6 and six in 0.1. Entry and exit occur together in 13.1 percent of periods, entry only in 4.8 and exit only in 2.0, so entry and exit are positively correlated, which models without idiosyncratic uncertainty cannot generate. About 4 percent of jobs are destroyed and created each year, with a standard deviation twice the mean.

  • Lifetimes: 1,800 firms were ever active. The share exiting after one period is 48.3 percent and after two periods 24.7 percent; 89.1 percent are gone within ten periods. The median lifespan is 2, the mean 18.4 and the standard deviation 73.2. The hazard falls from 48.3 percent in the first period to 5.9 percent in the seventh.

  • Realized values: the mean discounted realized value is 0.69, close to the entry cost as free entry requires, the median is −0.1-0.1−0.1 and the standard deviation 4.09. Only 170 firms (9.4 percent) have positive values, with a mean of 10, fifty times the entry cost; 1,630 have negative values, with a mean of −0.27-0.27−0.27. The largest values are 72.8, 52.6 and 33.1, and about 3 percent of firms earn 57 percent of all positive realized values. Active firms have average per-period profits of 5.42 and an average market value over 20, a pure selection effect.

  • Shape of the value function: in the firm's own ω\omegaω the value function is first convex and then concave. Investment is low at low states, which drift down and exit, rises up to the inflection point and falls beyond it, so mortality is high at first and very low for firms that have passed the inflection point.

  • Concentration and markups: the share of the largest firm has mean 0.39, median 0.34 and standard deviation 0.11, with a 0.95 quantile of 0.62. The sales-weighted price-cost ratio has mean 1.33 and lies between 1.27 and 1.44 in 90 percent of periods. Without any external change the industry alternates between fragmented epochs and epochs dominated by one firm, for example forty periods in which the leading share averages about 0.6.

Policy Experiments and Welfare

Welfare numbers are means over 100 simulation runs, each starting from one firm at ω=4\omega=4ω=4; standard deviations across runs are in parentheses.

  • Markov-perfect Nash: firm cash flows 70 (26), consumer benefits 301 (65), total 369 (68). Average investment is 2.57 and the average number of active firms 3.4.

  • Single-product monopoly: cash flows 207 (66), consumer benefits 96 (17), total 303 (83), about 20 percent below free entry. A 20-period monopoly followed by free entry gives 180, 140 and 320, and a 10-period monopoly 146, 186 and 331.

  • Perfect collusion: cash flows 218 (55), consumer benefits 115 (19), total 332 (74), only 10 percent below the Nash solution because the cartel offers product variety. Two firms are active in 75.6 percent of periods and three in 23.1; investment averages 1.75, the number of firms 2.3, the leading share 0.60 and the price-cost ratio 2.30.

  • Social planner: total welfare 377, about 2 percent above Nash. Two firms are active in 49.6 percent of periods, three in 44.5 and four in 5.8; entry or exit occurs in 15.4 percent of periods against 20.1 under Nash and 14.2 under collusion. Investment averages 1.95, the number of firms 2.6 and the leading share 0.54; the price-cost ratio is one. Of 1,301 firms ever active the mean lifespan is 19.5.

  • Market-share cap: with σ∗=0.65\sigma^*=0.65σ∗=0.65 cash flows are 61.7, consumer benefits 289.7 and total 349.6, a fall of over 5 percent, while the structure statistics are nearly identical to the base case (investment 2.56, 3.4 firms, mean leading share 0.38, mean price-cost ratio 1.32). The cap binds in just under 1 percent of periods, against about 4 percent of unrestricted periods with a share of at least 0.65. With σ∗=0.55\sigma^*=0.55σ∗=0.55 the totals are 54.4, 284.8 and 337.5, a fall of about 9 percent.

  • Entry cost of 2: cash flows 76.5, consumer benefits 293.4 and total 361.5, and 369.3 once the discounted incremental entry fees of 7.8 are counted as transfers. Market structure changes sharply: two firms are active in 81.4 percent of periods and three in 17.1, entry or exit occurs in 1.6 percent of periods and the two become negatively correlated, the mean lifespan rises to 191.5 (median 6), investment falls to 1.97 and the number of firms to 2.2, the mean leading share rises to 0.51 with standard deviation 0.09, and the mean price-cost ratio is 1.41.

Three lessons follow. The Nash investor and entrant ignore the profits they take from rivals, so free entry yields more products and more investment than the planner chooses, whereas the cartel ignores consumer surplus and chooses fewer of both than the planner. The planner's market structure therefore lies close to the cartel's, and the two differ mainly in prices. Second, the standard deviation of welfare across runs within a regime is about 20 percent of its mean, twice the mean gap between collusion and free entry, which warns against case-study comparisons of regimes. Third, the share cap has a large welfare effect and an imperceptible effect on market structure while the entry cost does the opposite, so descriptive measures of market structure are not a reliable guide to welfare. The authors stress that the parameters were chosen more or less arbitrarily and that the results are illustrations.

Polynomial Approximation

For industries with many firms the pointwise calculation must be replaced. The proposal is to compute the value function only at a set of basis points ωj\omega^jωj and to predict it elsewhere from a fitted polynomial of order λ\lambdaλ with basis functions w(⋅)w(\cdot)w(⋅) and coefficients α\alphaα:

V^i−1[ω∗]=w(ω∗)′αi−1αi=[W′W]−1W′V∗i(26)\begin{aligned} \hat{V}^{i-1}[\omega^*]&=w(\omega^*)'\alpha^{i-1}\\ \alpha^i&=[W'W]^{-1}W'V^{*i} \end{aligned} \tag{26}V^i−1[ω∗]αi​=w(ω∗)′αi−1=[W′W]−1W′V∗i​(26)

The first line replaces Vi−1V^{i-1}Vi−1 in the Bellman equation, the Kuhn-Tucker condition and the entry value at the basis points, which yields updated policies and an updated value V∗iV^{*i}V∗i at those points. The second line refits the coefficients by least squares, where WWW stacks the rows w(ωj)′w(\omega^j)'w(ωj)′. An unrestricted polynomial still needs a number of basis functions that grows polynomially in NNN. Restricting attention to polynomials that are symmetric in (ω2,…,ωN)(\omega_2,\dots,\omega_N)(ω2​,…,ωN​) gives a space whose dimension satisfies:

dim⁡VλE≤∑p=0λ∑i=0pΔ(i)≡φ(λ)(27)\dim\mathcal{V}^{\mathcal{E}}_{\lambda}\leq\sum_{p=0}^{\lambda}\sum_{i=0}^{p}\Delta(i)\equiv\varphi(\lambda) \tag{27}dimVλE​≤p=0∑λ​i=0∑p​Δ(i)≡φ(λ)(27)

with equality when N−1≥λN-1\geq\lambdaN−1≥λ (the paper states N≥λN\geq\lambdaN≥λ, but splitting the order λ\lambdaλ into λ\lambdaλ ones needs λ\lambdaλ competitors), where Δ(i)\Delta(i)Δ(i) is the number of partitions of the integer iii. The reason is that a symmetric polynomial has one free coefficient for each own exponent and each unordered allocation of the remaining order among the competitors. The first-order basis functions are ω1\omega_1ω1​ and ∑i≥2ωi\sum_{i\geq2}\omega_i∑i≥2​ωi​. The bound φ(λ)\varphi(\lambda)φ(λ) does not depend on NNN: it is 75 for order 6 and 890 for order 12 (the paper's Table 8 reports 854, which rests on miscounted partition numbers), against 639,000 grid points in the pointwise calculation. In a one-step test with sixth-order polynomials the fit was about equally good for any number of firms and nearly as good when the coefficients were fitted on a small subset of points. The implied policies reproduced total investment, the average price-cost ratio, the mean leading share and welfare almost exactly, but did less well for the discrete entry and exit policies: five or more firms were active at about 15 percent of points against 3 percent in the exact solution.

This is the primitive of the static demand side: the indirect utility that consumer rrr obtains from buying one unit of good jjj. The term vjv_jvj​ is the quality of good jjj (common to all consumers), pj∗p^*_jpj∗​ is its price in money units, and ϵrj\epsilon_{rj}ϵrj​ is a consumer-specific taste shock. Utility is linear in price with a coefficient normalized to one, so quality is measured in money units and there are no income effects. The index jjj runs over 0,1,…,N0,1,\dots,N0,1,…,N, where good 000 is the outside good, and each of the MMM consumers buys the single good with the highest UrjU_{rj}Urj​.

Only utility differences matter for choice. Consumer rrr prefers jjj to qqq when

ϵrj−ϵrq≥[vq−v0]−[vj−v0]+[pj∗−p0∗]−[pq∗−p0∗]=g(ωq)−g(ωj)+pj−pq\epsilon_{rj}-\epsilon_{rq}\geq[v_q-v_0]-[v_j-v_0]+[p^*_j-p^*_0]-[p^*_q-p^*_0]=g(\omega_q)-g(\omega_j)+p_j-p_qϵrj​−ϵrq​≥[vq​−v0​]−[vj​−v0​]+[pj∗​−p0∗​]−[pq∗​−p0∗​]=g(ωq​)−g(ωj​)+pj​−pq​

with pq=pq∗−p0∗p_q=p^*_q-p^*_0pq​=pq∗​−p0∗​ and g(ωq)=vq−v0g(\omega_q)=v_q-v_0g(ωq​)=vq​−v0​. Subtracting the utility of the outside good from every alternative therefore gives the normalized utilities g(ωj)−pj+ϵrjg(\omega_j)-p_j+\epsilon_{rj}g(ωj​)−pj​+ϵrj​ for inside goods and ϵr0\epsilon_{r0}ϵr0​ for the outside good. This normalization is what makes the state ωj\omega_jωj​ a relative quality: it falls whenever v0v_0v0​ rises by more than vjv_jvj​, which is the source of the common negative shock ν\nuν in equation (6). The distribution is degenerate given the outside shock realized during the setup period: if the outside alternative does not improve (ν=0\nu=0ν=0) the entrant arrives at the kink point ω∗\omega^*ω∗ of equation (5), and if it improves (ν=1\nu=1ν=1) the entrant arrives one step lower. In other words the entrant is built at ω∗\omega^*ω∗ and is then hit by the same common shock as the incumbents, exactly as an incumbent at ω∗\omega^*ω∗ with ν1=0\nu_1=0ν1​=0 would move by equation (6):

ωe=ω∗−ν,Pr⁡{ωe=ω∗−1}=δ,Pr⁡{ωe=ω∗}=1−δ\omega_e=\omega^*-\nu,\qquad\Pr\{\omega_e=\omega^*-1\}=\delta,\qquad\Pr\{\omega_e=\omega^*\}=1-\deltaωe​=ω∗−ν,Pr{ωe​=ω∗−1}=δ,Pr{ωe​=ω∗}=1−δ

In the base case, with the monopolist's exit state normalized to one, ω∗=4\omega^*=4ω∗=4 and δ=0.7\delta=0.7δ=0.7, so entrants arrive at 3 with probability 0.7 and at 4 with probability 0.3.

The economic content is that the entry state is fixed in relative terms. Since ω\omegaω measures quality relative to the outside alternative, a fixed ω∗\omega^*ω∗ means that the absolute quality of new entrants improves at the pace of the outside world. If entrants instead arrived at a fixed absolute quality, their relative quality would drift down over time and entry would eventually stop. The distribution enters the value of entry in equations (9) and (18) and the planner's recursion in equation (25). Entry three or four steps above the exit state, combined with a 0.7 chance of moving down each period, is what produces the very high early mortality in the simulations.

The first part defines the state space of the industry. A structure sss is a vector of nonnegative integers, with sjs_jsj​ the number of active firms at efficiency j∈{1,…,K}j\in\{1,\dots,K\}j∈{1,…,K}. Efficiencies are confined to a finite set because firms exit below a lower threshold and stop investing above an upper one, and the total number of firms is at most N∗+m∗N^*+m^*N∗+m∗ because nobody enters once N∗N^*N∗ firms are active and at most m∗m^*m∗ enter per period. Counting multisets of size nnn drawn from KKK levels and summing over nnn gives the number of such vectors:

∣S∣=∑n=0N∗+m∗(K+n−1n)=(K+N∗+m∗N∗+m∗)<∞|S|=\sum_{n=0}^{N^*+m^*}\binom{K+n-1}{n}=\binom{K+N^*+m^*}{N^*+m^*}<\infty∣S∣=n=0∑N∗+m∗​(nK+n−1​)=(N∗+m∗K+N∗+m∗​)<∞

Finiteness is what makes pointwise computation possible, and the same counting argument reappears in equation (21).

The second part states the Markov property. The history st=(st,st−1,… )s^t=(s_t,s_{t-1},\dots)st=(st​,st−1​,…) matters for the future only through the current structure sts_tst​, because profits depend only on (ω,s)(\omega,s)(ω,s), the increments of equation (6) are independent over time, and strategies are restricted to depend on the payoff-relevant state. The object Q[s′∣s]Q[s'\mid s]Q[s′∣s] is therefore a finite transition matrix. It is the equilibrium object: every firm's perceived kernel qωq^{\omega}qω in equations (7) and (8) and every entrant's qm−1q_{m-1}qm−1​ in equation (9) must be the conditional distributions derived from QQQ, and the optimal policies computed under those perceptions must regenerate QQQ. Ergodicity of QQQ justifies describing the equilibrium by long simulations, as the note does for the base case.

whose left-hand side is increasing in μ\muμ, so the solution is unique. At given shares it exceeds the Nash markup of every product whenever n≥2n\geq2n≥2, and it rises with the number and quality of products. This is consistent with the simulated price-cost ratio of 2.30 under collusion against 1.33 under Nash. Joint profit increases when a product is added, which is why the cartel offers variety, but by less than the entrant's own profit, which is why it offers fewer products than free entry.

This is the exit (product-scrapping) step of the single decision maker's recursion. The planner or cartel starts the period with nnn products ordered from best to worst, ω1≥ω2≥⋯≥ωn\omega_1\geq\omega_2\geq\dots\geq\omega_nω1​≥ω2​≥⋯≥ωn​, and decides how many to keep. Keeping the qqq best ones yields Vˉi(ω1,…,ωq)\bar{V}^i(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)Vˉi(ω1​,…,ωq​), defined in equation (25), which already includes the scrap value (n−q)Φ(n-q)\Phi(n−q)Φ of the products dropped. The value at iteration iii is the best of the nnn options:

q∗=arg⁡max⁡q∈{1,…,n}Vˉi(ω1,…,ωq)q^*=\arg\max_{q\in\{1,\dots,n\}}\bar{V}^i(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)q∗=argq∈{1,…,n}max​Vˉi(ω1​,…,ωq​)

and n−q∗n-q^*n−q∗ products are withdrawn. Strictly, Vˉi\bar{V}^iVˉi depends on nnn as well as on the qqq states kept, through the term (n−q)Φ(n-q)\Phi(n−q)Φ; the notation suppresses this.

Two restrictions are built in. First, only the lowest-ranked products are candidates for scrapping. This is without loss: all products have the same scrap value and the same technology, and both the current benefit and the continuation value are nondecreasing in each ωj\omega_jωj​, so dropping a better product in place of a worse one can never help. The ordering reduces the exit decision from 2n2^n2n subsets to nnn alternatives. Second, qqq starts at one, so at least one product is always kept; the option of shutting the industry down (q=0q=0q=0, value nΦn\PhinΦ) is excluded.

This step replaces the individual exit rule max⁡{Φ,⋅}\max\{\Phi,\cdot\}max{Φ,⋅} of equation (8). The difference is that the decision maker compares Φ\PhiΦ with the product's contribution to joint surplus or profit, net of the business it takes from sibling products, whereas a Nash firm compares Φ\PhiΦ with its own value. Because there is one decision maker, the recursion is an ordinary dynamic program and no equilibrium beliefs are needed.

This is the value to the planner or cartel of keeping the qqq best products. It has three parts. The first is the current benefit B(ω1,…,ωq)B(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)B(ω1​,…,ωq​) of the products kept: for the cartel the maximal joint profit of equation (23), for the planner consumer surplus at prices equal to marginal cost, where profits are zero. Scrapped products do not sell in the current period, as in equation (8). The second is the scrap value (n−q)Φ(n-q)\Phi(n−q)Φ. The third is the better of two investment programmes, without and with the launch of a new product. In both, the decision maker chooses all investments (x1,…,xq)(x_1,\dots,x_q)(x1​,…,xq​) jointly at cost c∑jxjc\sum_jx_jc∑j​xj​, and the kept products move according to p(ωj′∣ωj,xj,ν)p(\omega'_j\mid\omega_j,x_j,\nu)p(ωj′​∣ωj​,xj​,ν), the law of motion (6) with ωj′=ωj+τj\omega'_j=\omega_j+\tau_jωj′​=ωj​+τj​, independently given the common shock ν\nuν. In the second programme the sunk cost xex_exe​ is paid now and the new product arrives next period at ωe\omega_eωe​ drawn from equation (11), so the continuation value has q+1q+1q+1 arguments (reordered). The sums are over ω1′,…,ωq′\omega'_1,\dots,\omega'_qω1′​,…,ωq′​, ν\nuν and, in the second, ωe\omega_eωe​.

The note's display corrects the paper's printed one in two places. The paper's left-hand side has last argument ωi\omega_iωi​, which clashes with the iteration index; ωq\omega_qωq​ is right, since the right-hand side depends on (ω1,…,ωq)(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)(ω1​,…,ωq​). More importantly, the paper prints no discount factor in front of the continuation values. Welfare and cartel profits are defined as discounted sums, and without discounting the iteration would not converge, so β\betaβ is required. The corrected recursion, which is the note's equation, is

Vˉi(ω1,…,ωq)=  B(ω1,…,ωq)+(n−q)Φ+max⁡{sup⁡(x1,…,xq)−c∑jxj+β∑Vi−1(ω1′,…,ωq′)p(ω1′∣ω1,x1,ν)⋯p(ωq′∣ωq,xq,ν)p(ν);sup⁡(x1,…,xq)−c∑jxj−xe+β∑Vi−1(ω1′,…,ωq′,ωe)p(ω1′∣ω1,x1,ν)⋯p(ωq′∣ωq,xq,ν)p(ωe∣ν)p(ν)}\begin{aligned} \bar{V}^i(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)=\;&B(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_q)+(n-q)\Phi\\ &+\max\Big\{\sup_{(x_1,\dots,x_q)}-c\sum_jx_j+\beta\sum V^{i-1}(\omega'_1,\dots,\omega'_q)p(\omega'_1\mid\omega_1,x_1,\nu)\cdots p(\omega'_q\mid\omega_q,x_q,\nu)p(\nu);\\ &\sup_{(x_1,\dots,x_q)}-c\sum_jx_j-x_e+\beta\sum V^{i-1}(\omega'_1,\dots,\omega'_q,\omega_e)p(\omega'_1\mid\omega_1,x_1,\nu)\cdots p(\omega'_q\mid\omega_q,x_q,\nu)p(\omega_e\mid\nu)p(\nu)\Big\} \end{aligned}Vˉi(ω1​,…,ωq​)=​B(ω1​,…,ωq​)+(n−q)Φ+max{(x1​,…,xq​)sup​−cj∑​xj​+β∑Vi−1(ω1′​,…,ωq′​)p(ω1′​∣ω1​,x1​,ν)⋯p(ωq′​∣ωq​,xq​,ν)p(ν);(x1​,…,xq​)sup​−cj∑​xj​−xe​+β∑Vi−1(ω1′​,…,ωq′​,ωe​)p(ω1′​∣ω1​,x1​,ν)⋯p(ωq′​∣ωq​,xq​,ν)p(ωe​∣ν)p(ν)}​

With β\betaβ in place, the map from Vi−1V^{i-1}Vi−1 to ViV^iVi defined by equations (24) and (25) satisfies Blackwell's conditions exactly as in equation (14), so it is a contraction of modulus β\betaβ and the iteration converges to the unique value function. This is why the paper calls the algorithm much simpler than the one for the game. Each xjx_jxj​ now weighs the gain to the whole portfolio, including the losses that a better product jjj inflicts on the sibling products, so there is no closed form like equation (17), and investment is lower than under Nash behaviour, as in the reported averages.

The first line is the approximating family: the value function is replaced by a polynomial, that is, a linear combination of known basis functions w(⋅)w(\cdot)w(⋅) (monomials in the states up to order λ\lambdaλ) with coefficient vector αi−1\alpha^{i-1}αi−1. Here ω∗\omega^*ω∗ denotes an arbitrary point of the state space (not the kink point of equation (5)), so the first line predicts Vi−1V^{i-1}Vi−1 at any point from a small number of coefficients.

The second line is a least squares fit. Given αi−1\alpha^{i-1}αi−1, use the first line in place of Vi−1V^{i-1}Vi−1 in equations (16), (18) and (19) at each of the JJJ basis points ω1,…,ωJ\omega^1,\dots,\omega^Jω1,…,ωJ to obtain updated values V∗i(ωj)V^{*i}(\omega^j)V∗i(ωj), and stack them in the vector V∗iV^{*i}V∗i. Let WWW be the JJJ-row matrix with rows w(ωj)′w(\omega^j)'w(ωj)′. The new coefficients minimize the Euclidean distance between the polynomial and the updated values at the basis points:

αi=arg⁡min⁡α∑j=1J[V∗i(ωj)−w(ωj)′α]2=arg⁡min⁡α(V∗i−Wα)′(V∗i−Wα)\alpha^i=\arg\min_{\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\left[V^{*i}(\omega^j)-w(\omega^j)'\alpha\right]^2=\arg\min_{\alpha}\left(V^{*i}-W\alpha\right)'\left(V^{*i}-W\alpha\right)αi=argαmin​j=1∑J​[V∗i(ωj)−w(ωj)′α]2=argαmin​(V∗i−Wα)′(V∗i−Wα)

Differentiating with respect to α\alphaα and setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations:

−2W′(V∗i−Wα)=0⟹W′Wα=W′V∗i-2W'\left(V^{*i}-W\alpha\right)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad W'W\alpha=W'V^{*i}−2W′(V∗i−Wα)=0⟹W′Wα=W′V∗i

If WWW has full column rank, which requires at least as many basis points as basis functions, W′WW'WW′W is invertible and

αi=[W′W]−1W′V∗i\alpha^i=[W'W]^{-1}W'V^{*i}αi=[W′W]−1W′V∗i

The second-order condition holds because W′WW'WW′W is positive definite. If the number of basis points equals the number of basis functions, WWW is square and αi=W−1V∗i\alpha^i=W^{-1}V^{*i}αi=W−1V∗i, so the polynomial interpolates the updated values exactly. The iteration is thus a fixed-point problem in α\alphaα, whose dimension is the number of basis functions and not the number of grid points; equation (27) shows how small that number can be made. Since WWW does not change across iterations, [W′W]−1W′[W'W]^{-1}W'[W′W]−1W′ is computed once.

The polynomial satisfies the symmetry condition (20) if and only if its coefficients do:

α(h1,h2,…,hN)=α(h1,hπ(2),…,hπ(N))\alpha(h_1,h_2,\dots,h_N)=\alpha(h_1,h_{\pi(2)},\dots,h_{\pi(N)})α(h1​,h2​,…,hN​)=α(h1​,hπ(2)​,…,hπ(N)​)

for every permutation π\piπ of (2,…,N)(2,\dots,N)(2,…,N). So a coefficient is determined by the own exponent h1h_1h1​ and by the unordered collection of the competitors' exponents (h2,…,hN)(h_2,\dots,h_N)(h2​,…,hN​). A basis of the symmetric space is obtained by adding up all monomials that share these two items, and the dimension is the number of distinct pairs.
